title: Nepal floods ‘defining moment’ for climate action: UN - Arab News
description: Nepal floods ‘defining moment’ for climate action: UN  Arab News
publisher.title: Arab News
full_article:
KATMANDU: Nepal’s devastating floods should be a turning point for global climate action, with the international community helping the Himalayan nation recover, a top UN official told AFP on Saturday.

The country suffered one of the worst disasters in its history on August 26, when a mountain collapse near the China border triggered catastrophic floods that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing.

Scientists said climate change played a significant role in that disaster.

Jorge Moreira da Silva, executive director of the UN Office for Project Services (UNOPS), which implements humanitarian and development projects, said he had witnessed “massive devastation” during a visit to affected communities.

Nepal, a largely rural country of 30 million people that contributes little to global greenhouse gas emissions, estimates reconstruction will cost $4.78 billion.

“This is a defining moment not only for Nepal, this is a defining moment for the international community,” Moreira da Silva told AFP in Katmandu.

“It’s not fair to ask a country that emits almost nothing of CO2 to suddenly pay alone the consequence of something that was not generated by the country,” he added.

“That’s why it’s fundamental that global solidarity is brought to this equation.”

- ‘Climate justice’ -

Moreira da Silva said reconstruction and resettlement must account for future climate risks, while the international community must “renew its commitment to climate.”

“It’s also about climate justice and climate responsibility,” he said, warning that low-emitting countries would continue to bear the brunt of climate change.

“This is going to happen unless those countries that emit the most... change their pathway,” he said.

Moreira da Silva said Nepal was rebuilding as global disruptions threatened food security. He also leads the UN task force for the Strait of Hormuz.

“The simultaneous disruption of the three maritime shock points... the Strait of Hormuz, in the Black Sea and in the Red Sea, poses a significant challenge, particularly on food security,” he said.

The UN and its humanitarian partners launched a $49.6 million appeal last month to provide emergency assistance to flood victims.

Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah told the United Nations last month that the flooding “was a warning to the world” about the growing dangers of climate change.

title: Campus organizations plan a fundraiser for tragedy in Nepal - The Trail Blazer
description: Campus organizations plan a fundraiser for tragedy in Nepal  The Trail Blazer
publisher.title: The Trail Blazer
full_article:
Morehead State University’s Nepali Student Association is fundraising for relief after a catastrophic flood that hit Rasuwa, Nepal on August 26 resulting in over 1,300 deaths and 6,000 missing people.

“Even when the news moves on, the need remains. It is never too late to help, and even a small action can make a difference,” said Depesh KC, president of the NSA.

The group, founded roughly two years ago, began fundraising after several members were personally impacted by the flooding back home.

“Our own members’ families have been affected,” said KC. “Their relatives, members of their family, they died. They lost their lives.”

KC said the members of NSA have been using campus resources to deal with the emotions of the loss of their family members.

The group started fundraising with t-shirts depicting mountains such as the ones in Nepal.

“The price of the t-shirts cost twenty dollars. For us, the shirts cost ten dollars so the profit from that will go to fund relief,” said KC.

NSA’s advisor, Steve Chen, said that MSU locals have been helping the Nepali students find the best ways to raise money.

“The BCM (Baptist Campus Ministry)s has been a tremendously kind host; they even helped set up the t-shirt fundraiser and helped them identify the best vendor,” said Chen.

NSA will host an all-day fundraiser in conjunction with Fazoli’s in Morehead on October 26 with the proceeds going to a relief fund.

“You can go and have dinner or whatever you want at Fazoli’s,” said KC. “They will keep twenty percent of that for fund relief.”

Chen said that the fundraisers may not produce enough money to make a big impact on the cost of damages in Nepal, but it is about the effort for the students.

“Some of those students come up with ideas, and it is all about the effort, not the actual monetary benefit,” said Chen. “They want to be involved in the process; they see how meaningful it is. They are far from home so they feel this is the least they can do.”

title: Bayesian model maps climate shocks on Nepal’s Terai cereal yields - Bioengineer.org
description: Bayesian model maps climate shocks on Nepal’s Terai cereal yields  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
Nepal’s Terai lowlands are often described as the country’s grain basin, a fertile alluvial plain bordering India where paddy, wheat, and maize together account for more than 70% of national cereal production. A new study published in Results in Engineering has now modeled, over 36 years, how temperature, rainfall, humidity, atmospheric pressure, and wind interact with the yields of these three cereals, using a Bayesian Vector Autoregression (BVAR) framework that explicitly quantifies uncertainty. The findings arrive at a moment when the region’s agriculture, which sustains livelihoods for over 60% of Nepal’s population and contributes more than one-third of national GDP, is becoming progressively sensitive to climate variability.

The research team, led by Nanda Kumar Tharu with Arsanchai Sukkuea and Pensiri Akkajit, assembled annual data from 1989 to 2024 covering 22 Terai districts. Climatic observations came from the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, while crop statistics were sourced from the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development and cross-validated against the National Statistics Office and Open Data Nepal. Eighteen climatic variables were considered, including precipitation, surface pressure, absolute and relative humidity, air and wet-bulb temperatures, maximum and minimum daily temperatures, land surface skin temperature, and wind speeds measured at 10 and 50 meters above ground.

A central methodological challenge was aligning climate data with crop biology. Rather than averaging weather over whole calendar years, the researchers weighted climatic variables according to crop-specific growing seasons: June to November for paddy, November to April for wheat, and March to September for maize. District-level values were aggregated to regional averages using area-weighted means based on the cultivated area of each crop, ensuring that agriculturally intensive districts contributed proportionally to the regional signal. Missing station-level gaps, which represented less than 2% of observations, were filled by linear interpolation, and annual yields were temporally disaggregated to monthly frequency using proportional allocation derived from crop growth stages.

Before estimation, the team confronted multicollinearity, the natural interdependence among temperature, humidity, pressure, and wind variables. An iterative Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) analysis eliminated redundant predictors, retaining only variables with VIF values below 10. Three separate crop-specific BVAR models were then estimated, each with seven endogenous variables and two lags, yielding a parameter-to-observation ratio of 0.42, well within statistical limits. The Minnesota prior was adopted to regularize the models, shrinking coefficients toward zero with stronger shrinkage applied to longer lags and cross-variable effects. Crucially, the prior’s hyperparameters were treated hierarchically, specified as Half-Cauchy distributions and estimated from the data rather than fixed arbitrarily.

Estimation relied on the No-U-Turn Sampler, an adaptive variant of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, run across four Markov chains for 10,000 iterations each, producing 20,000 retained posterior samples. Convergence diagnostics were excellent: Gelman-Rubin statistics hovered near 1.0 for all parameters across all crops, effective sample sizes exceeded 400, and the Geweke diagnostic flagged only minor deviations in isolated cases. Sensitivity analyses varying the hyperparameters across plausible ranges confirmed that the ranking and direction of climate effects remained consistent, with coefficient variations below 5%. Alternative Cholesky orderings for the impulse response analysis, including crops-first and mixed arrangements, produced nearly identical results, with variations under 5%.

The impulse response functions revealed strikingly crop-specific sensitivities. Paddy yield responded most strongly to land surface skin temperature, declining by 0.456 t ha⁻¹ per one-standard-deviation shock, while maximum temperature and atmospheric pressure increased productivity by 0.441 and 0.418 t ha⁻¹ respectively. The authors interpret the positive temperature association cautiously, noting that moderate warming within the observed range can remain favorable for rice growth, consistent with field evidence from Tarahara, Nepal, where temperature increases of up to 2 °C benefited paddy before thresholds were exceeded. Negative associations with humidity and relative humidity align with known disease mechanisms, since humid microclimates favor pathogens such as Magnaporthe oryzae, the causal agent of rice blast.

Wheat emerged as the most wind-vulnerable crop. Wind speed variability at 50 meters showed a strong negative association with yield, and the forecast error variance decomposition identified wind-related variables as dominant drivers, with minimum wind speed at 50 meters contributing 28.4% and maximum wind speed at 10 meters contributing 22.1% of yield variability. The agronomic mechanisms are well documented: strong winds during heading and grain filling can cause lodging, accelerate evapotranspiration, and induce moisture stress even when soil water is adequate. Maize, by contrast, displayed moderate resilience, responding positively to maximum temperature and pressure but declining under excessive wind variability, high humidity, and elevated wet-bulb temperature, patterns consistent with heat stress effects on pollen viability and waterlogging constraints on root respiration.

Forecast performance varied by evaluation criterion. Maize achieved the highest point-forecast accuracy, with a mean absolute percentage error of 5.24% and RMSE of 0.214 t ha⁻¹, while paddy achieved the best probabilistic performance with the lowest log predictive score, indicating that its predictive distribution better represented observed outcomes and uncertainty. Benchmark comparisons showed the BVAR consistently outperformed classical VAR, ARIMA, and naive persistence models, with RMSE reductions of 13–16%, 9–13%, and 20–28% respectively. External validation against independent 2024 statistics from the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development revealed percentage errors of −1.54% for paddy, −4.29% for wheat, and +3.58% for maize, all below 5%.

Perhaps the most consequential results concern the future. Under the low-emissions SSP1–2.6 scenario, all three cereals were projected to gain moderately by 2050, with increases of 7.4% for paddy, 9.4% for wheat, and 10.0% for maize. Under the intermediate SSP2–4.5 pathway, gains shrank, with wheat rising only 2.1%. Under the high-emissions SSP5–8.5 scenario, associated with a 3.2 °C temperature increase and 15% precipitation decline by 2050, yields were projected to fall by 11.9% for paddy, 18.0% for wheat, and 15.2% for maize. Wheat’s largest projected decline is consistent with its stronger historical associations with wind and temperature extremes, and the authors emphasize that these are scenario-conditional projections rather than guaranteed outcomes.

The study’s limitations are acknowledged by the authors: the model does not explicitly incorporate soil properties, irrigation infrastructure, fertilizer use, crop management, technological change, or pest dynamics, due to the lack of consistent long-term district-level data, and the estimated climate effects should be read as conditional associations rather than fully isolated causal effects. Chow tests detected significant structural shifts for wheat and maize around 2020, coinciding with the COVID-19 pandemic, though the authors note that supply-chain disruptions may be confounded with climatic and technological factors. Nevertheless, the framework demonstrates the value of hierarchical Bayesian inference for climate–yield forecasting in data-limited environments, and the authors argue that integrating such probabilistic forecasts into early-warning systems, seasonal climate services, and agricultural insurance could strengthen climate-risk management and national food security as the Terai’s agroecosystems face accelerating monsoon variability and thermal stress.

title: Nepal’s floods and avalanches are India’s early warning - The New Indian Express
description: Nepal’s floods and avalanches are India’s early warning  The New Indian Express
publisher.title: The New Indian Express
full_article:
There is no such thing as an easy mountain.

In 2022, I was choosing my first 8,000-metre peak. Manaslu was the obvious candidate, the peak climbers around the world call the gentle introduction to the giants. That autumn, Nepal issued a record 404 permits for it, and with support teams, somewhere between 700 and 1,000 people were on its slopes.

On 26 September, an avalanche between Camps 3 and 4 killed Anup Rai, a 34-year-old Nepali climber carrying oxygen up to Camp 4. The same day, Hilaree Nelson, whom her sponsor called the most prolific ski mountaineer of her generation, triggered a small slide while skiing from the summit and fell to her death. Six days later, another avalanche flattened tents at base camp. Even Ralf Dujmovits, one of the most experienced high-altitude climbers alive, turned back in the wind and snow.

In 2024, I chose Annapurna instead to start my 8000m journey, and the mountain climbers whispered about. Manaslu taught me that no mountain is easy. The mountain makes the decisions. All we control is how ready we are when it does.

This autumn, Manaslu repeated the lesson. Heavy snow buried the mountain through September. On the night of September 19, an avalanche struck Camp 3 and buried Dhruba Jyoti Guha, a German climber of Indian origin, and his guide Phursemba Sherpa inside their tent. Theirs were the third and fourth deaths of the season. Within days, most expeditions had abandoned the mountain.

Three weeks later, the valley below paid its own price. At about 4 am on October 11, a torrent of mud and debris tore down the Budhi Gandaki in Gorkha. There had been no heavy rain that weekend. Authorities believe a dry landslide in Chumnubri dammed the river and then gave way. By 8.40 am, the river at Arughat stood above eight metres, against a danger mark of five. Between 35 and 40 houses were swept away, along with bridges, power towers and the construction camp of the 341 MW Budhi Gandaki hydropower project. Herders sheltering in sheds near the source are among the missing, and more than a hundred trekkers were stranded at Jagat.

title: Hundreds missing, including 47 Americans, in deadly Nepal floods, local officials say - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
description: Hundreds missing, including 47 Americans, in deadly Nepal floods, local officials say  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
publisher.title: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
full_article:
Serious flash flooding in Nepal on Wednesday morning has left over a hundred reported dead and hundreds more missing, including at least 47 American tourists, Nepali officials said, after a massive wall of water tore through a region on the Nepal-Tibet border.

The flooding, captured in dramatic video footage, occurred in the northern Rasuwa district, along the border with Tibet, at around 8:40 a.m. local time on Wednesday, authorities said, inundating coastal areas along the Trishuli River, burying some buildings and damaging bridges and roadways.

In a statement, Nepal's office of the prime minister expressed "deep sorrow" over the loss of life. "Offering heartfelt tribute to all those who lost their lives in this natural disaster, it extends its sincere condolences to the bereaved families and relatives," the statement shared on social media said.

Rescuers use an earthmover to carry a victim of flash flooding to safety along the Trishuli River in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo

Related Deadly Nepal flood caused by enormous landslide, glacier tumble: Scientist

The prime minister's office later said search and rescue operations carried out by the Nepali Army would continue through the night.

Nepali police said 162 were killed in the flood-affected areas, while Chinese state-run media Xinhua News Agency reported three dead. Authorities said the identification process is ongoing.

A resident walks along a street covered in mud following flash floods and a landslide disaster in Devghat, in Nepal's Nuwakot district, August 26, 2026. Prakash Mathema/AFP via Getty Images

At least 403 foreign nationals and 93 Nepali tourists are reported missing, according to the Prime Minister's Office of Nepal. Chinese media reported 265 missing.

The Nepali Tourism Board reported that the missing includes at least 47 American tourists who have been out of contact since floods hit the Rasuwa region.

The State Department said the number of Americans among the missing and otherwise impacted by the floods has fluctuated throughout the day, and that officials don’t yet have an accurate figure.

A drone view shows mud covering properties following a flash flood in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 27, 2026. Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters

"The United States extends its deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the devastating flash floods in the Rasuwa district of Nepal. Our thoughts are with all those affected by this disaster," a department spokesperson said in a statement issued later Wednesday.

The spokesperson said the State Department is "closely monitoring the situation and is deploying a disaster response advisor to the region to support response efforts. The Department will also provide $500,000 in assistance through its global award with Catholic Relief Services, supporting emergency shelter, relief items, and water, sanitation, and hygiene assistance to flood-affected communities."

Houses lie partially submerged in muddy water along a riverside after flash floods at Trishuli Bazar in Nepal's Nuwakot district on August 26, 2026. A massive flood swept through Nepal's northern Rasuwa district on August 26, damaging roads and power infrastructure as authorities scrambled to assess the scale of the destruction. Prabin Ranabhat/AFP via Getty Images

An influential Indian spiritual guru and entrepreneur known as Sadhguru said in a post on social media that 77 people who were on tours organized by his Isha Foundation were at an immigration center at the Nepal-Tibet border when the floodwaters came rushing in. Isha Foundation has confirmed to ABC News that 22 of the 77 people are Americans.

Rescuers gather on a rooftop as floodwaters sweep through Trishuli Bazar following a flash flood, in Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 26, 2026. Narendra Shrestha/EPA/Shutterstock

Many of them were traveling to or from Mount Kailash, a Himalayan peak near the border between Nepal and Tibet, an autonomous region of China. Mount Kailash, which is part of a Hindu pilgrimage called the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, is revered by many Hindus as the spiritual home of the god Shiva.

The Isha Foundation, which is headquartered in India, also has a base in McMinnville, Tennessee. The group's coordinator told ABC News the group has been in touch with family members in the U.S.

Three of the missing Americans were listed as traveling with a Nepali company called Fishtail Tours and Travel. The agency confirmed to ABC News that three American nationals are among the missing tourists traveling with them.

A drove view of mud covered properties following a flash flood at Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 26, 2026. Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters

Efforts to locate and rescue the missing tourists are ongoing, the company said, without providing any further information on their possible whereabouts or well-being.

The Nepal Tourism Board said that local tourism and law enforcement authorities were "working to verify the whereabouts and safety status of tourists and travelers who were in or traveling through the affected areas."

Nepali authorities have mobilized 656 police personnel to respond as of 7:30 p.m. local time, according to police.

A drone view shows mud covering properties following a flash flood at Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 26, 2026. Reuters

The flood was reportedly triggered by a landslide about 20 kilometers northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border post along the Nepal-China border, according to Nepal Disaster Management.

A 5.2-magnitude landslide impacted Nepal on Wednesday, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.

The seismic activity from the landslide was initially erroneously reported as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake, the agency said. It is unclear what triggered the landslide.

A geophysicist at New York's Columbia University told ABC News it appeared a landslide in the Himalayas took away a large glacier or parts of a glacier in the mountain pass.

The U.S. Embassy in Kathmandu said in posts to X that it was "deeply saddened by the tragic loss of life and devastation" caused by the flooding. "We are closely tracking developments and remain in close contact with Nepali authorities," the embassy said.

Also among the foreign nationals listed as missing in the Tourism Board's preliminary count were Indian, Malaysian, British, South African, Dutch and Australian tourists.

A boy looks at the devastation caused by flash flooding along the Trishuli River in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Aug. 26, 2026. Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo

Three army helicopters attempted to fly in to conduct relief operations Wednesday but had to turn back due to bad weather between Kathmandu, Nepal and the flooded areas, Sunil Sharma, spokesperson at Nepal Tourism Board, told ABC News.

Authorities are working to identify victims and conduct rescue efforts, and they hope rescue flights can resume tomorrow if the weather improves, Sharma said.

title: Nepali man learning from Japan to preserve flood-hit sites for posterity - Japan Wire by Kyodo News
description: Nepali man learning from Japan to preserve flood-hit sites for posterity  Japan Wire by Kyodo News
publisher.title: Japan Wire by Kyodo News
full_article:
"Rebuilding victims' lives is the top priority now, but we must also think about how to pass on the lessons for the next decade or so," said Prakash Poudel, drawing on his experiences visiting Hiroshima's Atomic Bomb Dome and a disaster museum in Kobe, the city hit hard by a huge quake in 1995.

Poudel, owner of a travel agency and a Japanese-language school in Kathmandu, visited Japan in 2009 and 2010. On both occasions, he was part of a program for Japanese-language teachers, touring the Atomic Bomb Dome twice and Kobe's Disaster Reduction and Human Renovation Institution once.

"I was shocked by the horror of the atomic bombing and the destructive power of earthquakes," Poudel said.

The dome was the only structure left standing near the hypocenter after the 1945 U.S. atomic bombing of Hiroshima, and its skeletal remains are preserved as a memorial. The Kobe facility tells the story of the 1995 earthquake that took more than 6,400 lives.

After seeing images of flood damage in Nepal's affected areas, including mud-covered riverbanks and damaged buildings, Poudel recounted what he observed in Japan and decided that the affected sites must be preserved to pass on the memory.

He said the idea came as he felt the memories of another disaster -- the 2015 earthquake which struck central Nepal and killed about 9,000 people -- seemed to be fading. He fears the same could happen with this summer's disaster.

In his proposal, buildings at risk of collapse would be torn down for safety, while the rest of the disaster-hit areas would be preserved with minimal work such as markers showing how high the floodwaters rose.

He also wants to build a facility for climate change researchers on higher ground near the site, where videos and photos of the landslides would be displayed.

Poudel plans to submit the proposal to Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah and government officials.

title: Rising costs make Dashain harder to celebrate happily - The Rising Nepal
description: Rising costs make Dashain harder to celebrate happily  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Oct. 18: Soaring prices of essential commodities, clothing and other consumer goods have made it increasingly difficult for people to manage their household budgets during Dashain and Tihar.

Rising fuel prices, higher transportation and production costs, expensive imports and growing festive demand have contributed to price increases across the market.

Besides, the prices of commodities have further increased in the market with the increasing demand of daily consumer goods, including rice, oil, lentils, vegetables, meat and fruits to clothes and leaving consumers hard pressed to manage budget for Dashain.

Supply chains disrupted by the Bhotekoshi flood on August 26 and subsequent rainfall in September have yet to return to normal, although supplies have gradually improved.

Consumers, however, continue to face higher prices, with some traders and middlemen reportedly taking advantage of supply constraints to increase prices.

Consumers said prices had been rising over the past year, making it increasingly difficult to afford festival expenses. Dashain is an occasion when many middle- and low-income families spend beyond their regular budgets, sometimes borrowing money to celebrate.

Essential goods become more expensive

Sandhya Pudasaini of Bhaisepati said the prices of essential commodities, including rice and edible oil, had increased significantly compared with last year. “I recently bought a 25-kg sack of the rice we regularly consume for Rs. 2,700, whereas it cost less than Rs. 2,500 almost a month ago,” she told The Rising Nepal.

She said prices of lentils and other household necessities had also risen considerably, adding to the financial burden during Dashain.

Amul Kazi Tuladhar, general secretary of the Nepal Retailers Association, said the prices of consumer goods, including rice and edible oil, had increased by 10 to 15 per cent over the past one to two months.

According to him, rice prices had risen by Rs. 15 to Rs. 20 per kg, depending on the variety, while edible oil had become around Rs. 30 per litre more expensive. Depending on the variety, edible oil now costs Rs. 250 to Rs. 340 per litre.

“Retailers sell goods at the maximum retail price (MRP), so we have little control over reducing or increasing prices. When we purchase goods from wholesalers, the MRP has already increased. Wholesalers tell us that the increases are due to import prices and transportation costs,” he said.

Tuladhar added that prices tended to rise during festivals as importers and wholesalers sought to benefit from increased demand.

Citing sugar as an example, he said its price had reached Rs. 160 per kg before the Salt Trading Corporation began supplying it to retailers at Rs. 105 per kg. Retailers then sold the sugar at Rs. 110 per kg, prompting suppliers to lower their prices. The example, he said, demonstrated that improved supplies could help bring prices down.

To provide relief to consumers, the Food Management and Trading Company Limited and the Salt Trading Corporation are selling essential commodities at discounted rates through their outlets across the country. They are offering discounts of Rs. 5 per kg or litre on products including rice, lentils, cooking oil, beans and sugar.

Vegetable prices have also increased in the Kathmandu Valley, adding to the expenses of households preparing for the festivals.

Garment prices surge by up to 20 per cent

Clothing has also become more expensive this year, adding to the financial pressure on festival shoppers.

Manoj Babu Shrestha, president of the Nepal National Traders’ Federation, said garment prices had increased by 15 to 20 per cent compared with last year, mainly due to the rise in the US dollar exchange rate and transportation costs.

However, he said the increase was not abnormal and that the federation had urged its members not to raise prices unreasonably.

According to Shrestha, transportation costs for goods imported from China through the Korala border have increased by 15 per cent compared with shipments previously routed through Tatopani and Rasuwagadhi.

Gayatri Banjara of Baneshwor said the prices of almost all clothing items had increased by Rs. 200 to Rs. 300 per piece compared with last year. The limited availability of new designs had also disappointed consumers.

Traders had told her that many garments imported from China were stranded in transit because of road blockage at various locations.

“I came to buy clothes for my children, but the prices have risen drastically,” she said, adding that she had been compelled to choose from the limited options available.

She spent around Rs. 15,000 on clothes and shoes for her two children.

Economist Dr. Chandra Mani Adhikari attributed the price increases to higher import, production and transportation costs, as well as supply shortages. He said disruptions caused by floods and landslides had reduced the availability of goods, creating opportunities for some traders to impose unjustified price increases.

Meat gets costlier

Meat is an important part of Dashain celebrations, particularly for non-vegetarian families. However, higher prices amid increased festive demand have made it more expensive for households to maintain their traditional meals.

Goat meat is selling for as much as Rs. 1,900 per kg this year, up from around Rs. 1,500 during last year's Dashain. Traders attribute the increase to higher prices of live goats, which are currently selling for Rs. 800 to Rs. 900 per kg, compared with Rs. 650 to Rs. 720 last year.

“Meat prices have reached the highest level ever recorded in the Kathmandu Valley,” said Hari Katuwal, a meat trader in Gatthaghar, adding that prices could rise further as demand increases after Astami.

Live chyangras are selling for Rs. 1,250 to Rs. 1,350 per kg, while mutton prices range from Rs. 1,600 to Rs. 1,800 per kg and could reach Rs. 2,000 during the peak festive period.

Katuwal said mutton prices had increased by around Rs. 400 per kg compared with last year, while farm-level prices of live goats had risen by Rs. 150 to Rs. 200 per kg.

He currently purchases live goats from farmers in Sindhupalchowk at Rs. 800 to Rs. 850 per kg, which directly affects retail meat prices.

No business, no enthusiasm among consumers

Disruptions at the northern border have further affected the availability of goods ahead of Dashain, leaving traders struggling to meet festive demand.

Following the closure of the Rasuwagadhi and Tatopani trade routes, hundreds of containers carrying goods from China have been stranded at border points, delaying the arrival of clothing and other festival-related products.

“Goods, including clothes intended for Dashain, have not arrived on time because the containers are stranded at the border. This has limited the availability of new products in the market and adversely affected business,” said Shrestha.

After the Rasuwagadhi border was closed following the Bhotekoshi flood on August 26, containers carrying goods to Nepal were diverted to Tatopani and Korala. However, the subsequent closure of the Tatopani border by the Chinese side disrupted transportation through that route as well. But only today, China has agreed to open it for three days.

Road damage at various locations along the Kaligandaki Corridor leading to Korala further hampered the movement of goods.

More than 600 containers carrying Dashain-related goods, including electronics, clothing, food items and fruits, have been stranded at Kerung. Shrestha said it was now impossible for these shipments to reach the market through the northern border before Dashain.

Traders dependent on Chinese imports have been forced to rely on existing stocks to meet festive demand, with little prospect of replenishing supplies in time. Although there is no outright shortage of garments, the limited variety has made it difficult for consumers to find products according to their preferences.

Business, already severely affected by the Gen Z movement last year, has deteriorated further, Shrestha said. Traders who invested substantial amounts in importing goods from China have suffered because their shipments have not reached the market in time.

“Traders have suffered losses because they have been unable to bring the goods they purchased to the market in time for Dashain.

They have also had to bear the interest costs on loans taken to import the goods while their investments remain tied up in unsold or stranded stock,” Shrestha said.

Economist Adhikari said that the declining purchasing power of consumers, caused by significant annual price hikes amid low-income growth, has weakened aggregate demand over the past few years, a trend that has continued this year.

The resulting decline in demand has had a cascading effect on the entire economy, from production to consumption, he said. Low demand even during the festival season could further affect economic activity, he added.

Low-income families face debt risks

Economist Dr. Adhikari said rising prices of food, clothing, transportation and other essentials were placing a disproportionate burden on middle- and low-income households, which spend a large share of their earnings on basic necessities.

According to Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB), consumer price inflation rose to 6.34 per cent in mid-September 2026, up from 1.87 per cent a year earlier.

Food and beverage inflation stood at 7.54 per cent, while non-food and services inflation reached 5.69 per cent during the review period.

“The prices of all items, including meat, have surged. The current price increases are beyond what low-income people can afford. Low-income and daily-wage families, who look forward to Dashain to eat meat and other special dishes and purchase clothes, are among the most affected and disappointed,” he said.

Adhikari said many Nepalis spent more than 35 per cent of their annual expenditure during the roughly one-and-a-half months period covering Dashain, Tihar and Chhath.

The concentration of spending during this period, combined with rising prices, could force families to borrow money to meet even their basic needs.

“There is no practical way to reduce the consumption of food and the purchase of clothes significantly, even when prices rise so much. A huge portion of household budgets will be spent on these items, forcing families to borrow money for health and education,” he said.

He criticised the government for failing to control prices through adequate supplies and effective market monitoring, allowing some traders to make excessive profits.

Adhikari said effective market supervision, action against unfair

pricing and an adequate supply of essential goods were necessary to protect consumers, particularly those struggling to meet their basic needs during the festive season.

BY A STAFF REPORTER, Kathmandu, Oct. 18: Nepal suffered a 24-run defeat against Canada in the ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup League 2 on Saturday, failing to chase a target of 257 at the Al Amerat Cricket Ground in Oman.

The defeat dealt a setback to Nepal’s campaign to finish in the top six and retain their One-Day International (ODI) status.

Nepal, who had beaten Canada by 24 runs in their first meeting of the series and then defeated hosts Oman by 113 runs, were unable to repeat those performances against a

Opted to bat first after winning the toss, Canada’s innings was built around a century from opener Yuvraj Samra, who scored 105 from 117 balls, striking 11 fours and 4 sixes.

Samra anchored the innings through the middle overs after Aaron Johnson contributed 36 off 53 balls. Samit Gohel made 17, while Harsh Thaker added a patient 34 from 57 deliveries.

Captain Hamza Tariq then lifted the scoring rate with 30 off 26 balls, helping Canada build a competitive total despite wickets falling in the latter stages. Canada were eventually all out for 256 in 50 overs.

Nepal’s bowlers shared the work, with Lalit Rajbanshi taking four wickets and Captain Sandeep Lamichhane claiming three.

Dipendra Singh Airee picked up two wickets, while Rohit Paudel accounted for Gohel. However, Samra’s innings gave Canada the platform they needed, and Nepal were left chasing 257 to win.

Nepal’s reply depended heavily on Arjun Kumal, who top-scored with 87 from 112 balls. He held the innings together while wickets fell at the other end, but the home side could not build the partnerships needed to stay on course.

Aasif Sheikh made 20 and Ishan Pandey scored 21, while Paudel, whose performance in the last two games had been commendable was dismissed for 18.

Dipendra offered resistance with 27, and Gulsan Jha added 21, but neither could turn the chase around. Karan KC remained unbeaten on 17, yet Nepal were bowled out for 232, falling 24 runs short of the target.

The defeat has immediate consequences for Nepal’s League 2 campaign. Before the match, Nepal had 28 points from 34 games, one point ahead of Canada, who had played 35 matches. The result takes Canada to 29 points from 36 games, while Nepal remain on 28 from 35 and could slip below their rivals in the standings.

Nepal now have one league match remaining, against Oman on October 19. A win would take them to 30 points and strengthen their prospects of finishing in the top six; another defeat would leave their position more precarious.

Nepal had already fallen out of contention for a top-four League 2 finish, which secures direct entry to the ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup Qualifier for 2027.

The lower-ranked teams must instead go through the Qualifier Play-off, making Nepal’s final league position important to their route forward in international one-day cricket.

With one match left, Nepal need a more complete batting performance, stronger partnerships and a disciplined bowling effort to close the Oman campaign positively and protect their longer-term ODI prospects.

title: Safe Screens For Kids - The Rising Nepal
description: Safe Screens For Kids  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Children are among the most vulnerable members of society. They learn quickly, but exposure to disturbing media content can affect their mental and emotional well-being. In an increasingly digital world, access to online information is unavoidable. However, children's addiction to harmful posts and videos must be controlled. Children's safety must not end at the boundaries of their homes, schools and communities but also extend to the increasing access to the digital world. During floods, landslides and other disasters, social media becomes an important source of information. Such information shared online can help alert the public but extensive exchange of graphic footage showing deaths, people being swept away by floodwaters and destroyed homes raises serious concerns about children's exposure to distressing materials.





A child in Kathmandu reportedly became frightened and cried after repeatedly watching flood-related videos on a parent's mobile phone. Such incidents should prompt greater attention to how children encounter disaster-related content online, particularly when they have limited ability to understand or process what they are seeing. The responsibility for addressing this problem cannot rest solely with parents. Although parental supervision, screen-time management and digital literacy are important, families cannot monitor every piece of content that appears on a screen. Social media companies must also take responsibility for how their platforms distribute sensitive material, particularly to younger users.





Nepal can also learn from other countries regarding the regulation of social media use among children. For example, Australia does not allow children under 16 to have social media accounts. Similarly, Denmark has also announced an agreement to introduce an age limit for certain platforms. These kinds of legal decisions can protect children from growing exposure to risk-related social media. However, age restrictions alone cannot address the problem. Nepal government should also study and take a cue from these instances. Rather than slapping a blanket ban without considering the country’s situation, the country should do some homework on how and which sites need to be monitored. Because social media cannot be blamed alone for creating distress but they can also use digital platforms to learn, communicate, access public information and understand events affecting their communities. Any restriction must therefore be balanced, enforceable and designed to protect children's interests without unnecessarily limiting their access to information.





The immediate priority should be to make online spaces safer for children. Social media companies should build better systems to identify and limit graphic content, stop repeatedly showing harmful videos to young users and act quickly on reports. Content about disaster victims should be treated with particular sensitivity, respecting the dignity and privacy of those affected, while allowing for responsible journalism and legitimate reporting in the public interest. The government must also clarify the responsibilities of relevant agencies and platforms, strengthen the implementation of existing child online safety guidelines and establish accessible mechanisms for reporting harmful material. The National Telecommunications Authority, the National Cyber Security Centre, child-rights organisations, schools and parents should work together to improve digital safety and public awareness. At the same time, children need guidance on how to respond when they encounter disturbing material. Parents and teachers also have a role in asking children whether they are distressed after watching some videos and encouraging them to speak about their experiences.

full_article:
From the foothills of the Himalayas to the Japanese dinner table Nepal is famous for Mount Everest and its majestic trekking routes. But in Kathmandu, another attraction is emerging: Japanese cuisine . Nepal's capital now boasts over 40 Japanese restaurants, serving everything from sushi and sashimi to traditional dishes. The growing presence of these establishments reflects not only evolving culinary tastes but also the deepening ties between Nepal and Japan. Behind many of these restaurants are Nepalese entrepreneurs who have lived, studied, or worked in Japan for extended periods. Upon returning home, they bring with them professional experience, culinary skills, and a desire to introduce the food culture they have been deeply connected to.

Arjun Adhikari is one of them. After 18 years living in Japan, he opened his first Japanese restaurant at the Park Village resort in Nepal in 2019. The Hokkaido restaurant group he developed now has 10 locations. Adhikari's story illustrates how experiences abroad can become a foundation for business ventures back home. The skills acquired during her time working in Japan were transformed into business opportunities, while also helping to bring Japanese cuisine closer to Nepalese diners. A serving of ramen at Hokkaido Ramen House in Kathmandu. This restaurant brings the flavors of Northern Japan to the Nepalese capital. Localized sushi in the heart of Kathmandu. The development of Japanese cuisine in Nepal is not simply a matter of replicating dishes from the Land of the Rising Sun. Some restaurants are adapting their menus to suit local ingredients and conditions.

In April 2026, chef Yasuhito Kosugi opened his Harima restaurant near Boudhanath in Kathmandu. Approximately 80% of the ingredients are locally sourced. Instead of relying entirely on the types of fish commonly used in Japanese sushi, the restaurant uses farmed salmon from Nepal to replace imported salmon or tuna. This approach demonstrates how cuisine can adapt to a new environment while retaining its essence. Local ingredients help the restaurant reduce its reliance on external suppliers, while also creating a unique Japanese culinary experience in Nepal. The shift is also evident in the customer base. Purna Bahadur Chaudari, who opened the Momotarou restaurant in the Thamel area in 1999, now owns three restaurants. While foreign diners used to play a significant role, now about half of his customers are Nepalese. This figure shows that Japanese cuisine is moving beyond serving tourists and the expatriate community. Sushi, once considered a relatively unfamiliar dish, is gradually finding its place in the culinary lives of the local people.

With approximately one million international visitors each year, Nepal has the potential to develop food services catering to diverse groups of diners. However, the appeal of Japanese cuisine in Kathmandu stems not only from tourism but also from the Nepalese people themselves who have had direct contact with Japanese culture. The human resource paradox between Nepal and Japan. The ties between the two countries are also evident in the flow of labor. By the end of 2025, more than 300,000 Nepalese will be living in Japan, making this community the fifth largest foreign group in the East Asian nation. In the food service sector, work experience in Japan is creating a skilled workforce that can contribute to the development of the restaurant industry upon returning home. As of March 2026, approximately 4,200 Nepalese citizens will hold Specified Skilled Worker status in the food service sector in Japan.
